name: Fatima Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three, and at Linden Tax I lead the restaurant accounts team, checking sales books against bank deposits and speaking to owners before they file. I like turning a winter loss into a clear plan for an owner; blurry till-sheet photographs and repeat data entry drain the afternoon. At home my partner Amara and I juggle two school-age children and a mortgage, so the school bell is in my diary too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to lead that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earned a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, then worked through enough busy seasons to recognise when a stock figure is wrong. I use AI every day to draft the first questions, but I verify the return myself and ask the team to challenge anything too neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients at Linden Tax that a useful invoice sorter is welcome, but I still want the final tax return tied to a person. Restaurant owners have enough surprises without a guessed stock figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to draft questions on restaurant accounts, then compare every number with the sales book. My team-lead pay is above the usual rate and we have around nine months of expenses saved, so a modest tool gain feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily draft-and-check routine and use the saved minutes to call owners before their filing deadline. I'd move fifty a month from pay into the family emergency account, because the mortgage does not care how quick a draft is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own income in this picture. I still watch the household budget because our two children have school costs that do not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the work satisfying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A restaurant owner once thought a winter loss meant the place was finished; I showed her the seasonal pattern and she could plan. I like turning a frightening number into a usable decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wears you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Poor photographs of till sheets, especially when the bottom line is missing. A tool that spots the missing part would save me a dull phone call, but guessing the line would create another one.

say: I'd welcome **invoice sorting** with a named signer on the return.
I'd use saved minutes for **owner calls** before filing.
think: My **daily AI drafts** are checked against original sales books.
Higher pay and **nine months saved** protect our mortgage today.
do: Keep **daily question drafts** with manual sales-book checks.
Save **fifty monthly** from wages in the family emergency account.
feel: I feel **calm** about keeping my lead salary.
S0.quote: Restaurant owners have enough surprises without a guessed stock figure.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is an established checked routine, while a modest sorter changes little about her paid role.
Higher lead pay and **nine months saved** support a calm baseline, though school costs and a mortgage remain.

steps.text: Keep daily AI question drafts and check restaurant sales books
Save fifty monthly from salary in family emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Linden Tax's partners a sample of the mistakes the new return writer makes before we sell faster filing to restaurants. The junior staff need paid time to learn the checks, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can get a new tool working quickly, but the partners might use it to fold two review desks into mine. I am well paid now, and my own lead salary could be cut if the firm stops charging for checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid vendor workshop to learn the new stock-reconciliation controls on closed restaurant files, with the partner approving access and another accountant checking errors. In the first year of steady change, if Linden cuts my lead pay, I'd apply for posted senior tax posts at nearby firms and keep any paid Linden work until a written offer names a mortgage-covering wage and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own pay being reduced. The nine-month reserve gives us options, but I don't want the children's savings to become a salary substitute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners deny paid workshop time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with our approved daily drafting tool and ask them to put the new checking target in writing. I won't feed live restaurant sales into a system from my kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you judge the new controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count wrong stock totals and how long a person takes to repair them. If the method holds up, I'd use it, but I won't sign a return I haven't checked.

say: I'd test **wrong stock totals** before promising faster filing.
I'd ask for **paid learning time** for the review team.
think: A merged desk could cut my **lead salary** even if I learn the software quickly.
Our reserve cannot serve as a **permanent wage** while the children and mortgage need money.
do: Learn **stock controls** in an approved paid supervised workshop; use only after measured stock-error and repair-time checks pass.
Apply for **posted nearby tax** roles if Linden cuts lead pay.
Keep **paid Linden hours** until a written mortgage-covering offer starts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own pay.

fieldNote: The **new learning** concerns stock controls, not the daily question drafting she already knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our restaurant clients that full AGI in 2028 reaches the thinking in their tax records before robots reach kitchens around 2031. A recipe or a till sheet cannot make my desk safe for three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Linden to cut many senior reviews, perhaps my own lead post. We have a strong reserve and a lot of firms nearby, but my salary is a large part of our mortgage payment and those firms face the same technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone our planned second car and add ninety from each month's wages to the emergency account now. In the first year after 2028, if Linden ends my role, I'd apply for advertised salaried finance posts at the local food distributor and keep only any paid Linden closeout hours still offered until a written mortgage-covering wage, start date and school-compatible hours are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large loss of my own earnings. Nine months saved helps us search, but it cannot tell me the distributor will post a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the food distributor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've checked stock and supplier accounts for restaurants for years, so I could read its figures. AGI reaches those office tasks as well, so I'd take a real paid vacancy only, not a promise of safer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who handles the children if a new job starts early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Amara can take the morning school run on her later-start days. I'd accept only confirmed distributor hours that fit that arrangement; I won't assume her work schedule will change for me.

say: I'd say **2028 tax thinking** changes before kitchen robots around 2031.
I'd avoid calling food-office work **automatically safe**.
think: I expect my **lead post** may end quickly when Linden cuts senior tax review.
Nearby firms may face **similar AGI cuts** despite the number of local openings.
do: Postpone the **second car** and save ninety monthly from wages.
Apply for **posted distributor finance** if Linden ends my role.
Keep **offered paid Linden closeouts** until written mortgage-covering wage/start and distributor hours fit Amara’s confirmed school-run schedule.
S2.quote: Nine months saved helps us search, but it cannot tell me the distributor will post a vacancy.
fieldNote: The postponed car adds **ninety monthly** from wages, while the outside search begins only after actual job loss.
Distributor finance needs an **advertised salaried vacancy**, written mortgage-covering pay and start, and confirmed school-compatible hours; Linden pay lasts only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to spend the extra years finding which corrections restaurants will actually pay us to own. Full AGI reaches our tax desk in 2031, and physical kitchen robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn the tools, but I don't control the fees. If clients buy instant returns and stop paying for review, being fast at detecting errors may still leave me with no salaried post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a quarterly count of paid stock corrections and ask Linden for a written fee plan by each tax season. In the first year after 2031, if the firm cannot fund my lead salary from those fees, I'd apply for posted salaried distributor-finance roles and retain available paid Linden hours until a written mortgage-covering wage, start date and school-compatible schedule are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about paid work surviving, even with five years to prepare. Our reserve gives me room to refuse a poor offer, not permission to ignore the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for the distributor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification already. I'd take its required stock-control module only if a posted paid job calls for it and the employer funds the fee and paid study time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Linden's clients won't pay for corrections?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the figures early, then search posted roles rather than wait for my salary to stop. I'd keep any paid Linden assignments while they exist, but I wouldn't perform free review to keep a title.

I'd distinguish **2031 desk risk** from 2034 kitchen robots for restaurant clients.
think: My speed matters only if **clients fund** an accountable lead review role.
The reserve lets me **refuse weak terms** without missing the mortgage immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to make the mortgage lighter and to see whether clients still pay for accountable tax review. Full AGI reaches our desk in 2036; kitchen robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may have older children, but I will still need a salary. If restaurant clients stop paying for our lead checks, my ability with software will not create wages by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add one hundred and fifty each month from wages to our emergency account while both household jobs hold and review the paid-correction totals with the partners each year. In the first year after 2036, if Linden cannot fund my lead salary, I'd apply for posted salaried distributor-finance roles and retain any offered paid Linden hours until a written mortgage-covering wage, start date and school-compatible hours are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about needing a wage after 2036. Nine months saved today is strong, but one mortgage and two children can still use it up if income stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Amara's hours fall before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the extra saving and put current pay toward the mortgage and food. A ten-year plan cannot take precedence over this month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start your own tax service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on speculation. I am well paid at Linden now, and a private service would need paying clients and time I haven't promised away from the children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Linden could cut my lead salary before I find another paid post. A real advertised distributor vacancy with written wages, hours and a start date that work with school pickup would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the stock figure when a restaurant owner cannot see how it was made. A fast number can cost a family business a whole season.

headlineQuote: A fast number can cost a family business a whole season.
portrait: Fatima leads **restaurant tax accounts** at Linden and likes giving owners a clear plan.

Higher pay, **nine months saved**, nearby firms and two children support a strong but finite cushion.
She tests new controls on **paid supervised time** and tracks whether clients finance reviews.
AGI may end her **lead salary**; distributor work needs posted terms and school-compatible hours.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028** ending her lead salary before another paid role begins.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **real posted vacancy** with written mortgage-covering pay, start and school-compatible hours.
